live.name: MageCart
live.headline: MageCart: a threat actor listed in the MISP galaxy
live.in_short: MageCart is listed in the MISP galaxy catalogue. The record gives no aliases and no tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: MageCart is a threat actor named in the MISP galaxy catalogue.
The catalogue record lists no aliases and no tools for it.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: MageCart
next.headline: MageCart: card-skimming code planted on online checkout pages, run by many groups since at least 2018
next.in_short: MageCart is a name for web skimming. Attackers put JavaScript on checkout pages to copy card details. Reports describe many groups using it, against shops, platforms and their suppliers, from Newegg in 2018 to a 24-month campaign.

sentences.t: Malpedia describes Magecart as a malware framework meant to steal credit card information from compromised eCommerce websites.
Trend Micro says multiple groups are using the Magecart code, which it describes as a piece of malicious JavaScript.
Headlines in Malpedia's reference list name several groups, among them Magecart Groups 4, 8 and 12, Keeper, ATMZOW and Mirrorthief.
eSentire says FIN7 is one of many cyber gangs seen taking part in Magecart attacks.
WIRED reported in 2019 that Magecart hackers were casting the widest possible net to find vulnerable ecommerce sites.

Trend Micro lists victims that range from big e-commerce brands such as Newegg to a global ticketing site, Ticketmaster. It also cites online campus stores serving nearly 200 universities in the US and Canada.
Article headlines in Malpedia's list point to a campaign that infected 311 restaurants on online ordering platforms, and to one aimed at Spain.

ANY.RUN says the victims of one campaign were mostly retail e-commerce sites, in at least 12 countries and concentrated in Spain, France and the United States. It says banks, not merchants, bear the primary impact.
Malpedia says the first stage is typically JavaScript on a compromised checkout page. That script copies data from input fields and sends it to command and control servers.
Malwarebytes describes skimmers where a single line of code on a hacked shop loads remote JavaScript. A fake iframe is laid over the payment form, and stolen data is sent back in encoded form.

Malwarebytes found Magecart-linked skimmers hosted on the Heroku cloud platform. It earlier documented skimmers served from GitHub and Amazon S3 buckets. The report says the Heroku instances were reported and taken down.

Trend Micro lists three tactics: infecting third-party companies that supply code to other sites, scanning the internet for unsecured servers, and writing skimming code that works across many payment pages.

Sucuri says the ATMZOW skimmer is planted through Google Tag Manager containers. In late 2023 its operators used heavy obfuscation, base64 encoding and 40 newly registered domains, many hidden behind a firewall.
ANY.RUN describes a campaign that hijacked multi-step checkouts, imitated payment pages including Redsys in Spain, and sent card data out over WebSocket.
Sansec says a Linux trojan called CronRAT hides in scheduled tasks set for February 31st. It says CronRAT enables server-side Magecart card theft on eCommerce servers.

RiskIQ reported that Magecart operators registered a lookalike domain on August 13th, 2018. The skimmer on Newegg's checkout page became active around August 14th and was removed on September 18th, so customers were exposed for over a month.
RiskIQ says the Newegg skimmer code was recognisable from the British Airways incident.
In May 2019, CSIS notes, Trend Micro reported a campaign affecting 201 campus online stores in the US and Canada. Trend Micro gave that actor the name Mirrorthief.
WIRED reported in July 2019 that the group had hit 17,000 domains in a few months. It named British Airways and Ticketmaster among past hacks.

In October 2019, hackers breached Volusion, a provider of cloud-hosted online stores, and altered a file on its Google Cloud infrastructure. The report says more than 6,500 stores were affected and the number could be higher. It calls this a Magecart-style supply-chain attack.
ANY.RUN says one large Magecart-style campaign was active for at least 24 months and was supported by over 100 domains.
Sucuri advises treating unexpected scripts as a sign of compromise.
Shop owners should keep track of every third-party script on checkout pages and remove any they cannot explain.
